title: Emergency GPU Rotation & Cluster Stabilization — Playbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This runbook is a pragmatic, on-call facing guide for handling urgent GPU node issues that impact inference capacity: hardware GPU failure, driver/kernel corruption, or noisy neighbors requiring immediate GPU rotation and cluster stabilization. Focus is on minimizing customer impact (latency/queued requests) and ensuring safe hardware swaps or node replacements.

Scope:
- Applies to Dedicated and Private clusters managed by SRE (k8s + containerd + NVIDIA GPU stack).
- Covers immediate triage, safe cordon/drain, temporary capacity injection, GPU physical swap guidance for ops, and post-incident followup.
- Not a hardware-level procurement doc — coordinate with Hardware Ops for replacement parts.

Quick triage (first 10 minutes):
1) Observe alerts: which metric fired (GPU ECC errors, MIG eviction, node OOM, driver crash, GPU-util stuck at 0).
2) Check cluster state:
   - kubectl get nodes -o wide | egrep "gpu|accelerator"
   - kubectl describe node <node> | egrep -i "gpu|taint|unschedulable|kubelet"
3) Check node GPU state (if SSH available):
   - ssh core@<node-ip>
   - nvidia-smi -q | head -n 30
   - dmesg | egrep -i "NVRM|gpu|nvidia|oom" | tail -n 200
4) Is the node still serving inference containers? Check pod distribution and queue depth. If pods are stuck scheduling or failing ready checks, proceed to cordon/drain.

Decision matrix (high level):
- If GPU reports ECC or driver panic and pods are failing: cordon & drain immediately.
- If transient noise (spikes but no pod failures): monitor 5–15 min, consider enabling model fallback routing instead of draining.
- If multiple nodes in a rack show correlated failures -> escalate to Hardware Ops and treat as possible power/cooling issue.

Safe cordon + drain sequence (recommended on-call sequence):
1) Notify #sre-oncall and post to incident channel with basic facts: node, region, symptoms, ETA for drain.
2) kubectl cordon <node>
   - Ensure no new pods schedule.
3) Move critical stateful pods first (if any), otherwise drain: 
   - kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force --grace-period=120 
   - For long-running pods with PVs, coordinate with owners; consider scheduling to a maintenance node.
4) Watch pod evictions: kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
5) If pod fails to reschedule because of resource constraints -> inject capacity (see Capacity Add below) or rollback canary traffic.

Emergency GPU rotation (hardware ops handoff):
- Preconditions (before hardware team starts): node cordoned & drained, incident channel has hardware ops tagged, ticket created (HW-<ticket-id>).
- Provide to Hardware Ops: chassis ID, rack/u location, serial numbers (from asset db), last_kmsg/dmesg output, nvidia-smi logs.
- If physical swap is possible on hot-swap (depends on rack): ops may remove GPU, reseat/test, or replace.
- Minimum validation post-swap (ops): boot to runlevel, confirm drivers load, run nvidia-smi -L, run a small CUDA smoke test.
- Once hardware team signals ready -> node to SRE for rejoin: reboot if required, or system checks.

Node rejoin checklist (SRE):
1) ssh core@<node-ip> (or use fleet agent) -> check kernel modules: lsmod | egrep "nvidia|nv_peer_mem"
2) Verify GPU visible: nvidia-smi -L
3) Check container runtime health: sudo systemctl status containerd; sudo journalctl -u containerd -n 200
4) kubelet health: sudo systemctl status kubelet; kubectl get node <node> 
5) Remove any temporary taints: kubectl uncordon <node>
6) Observe pod placement & health; ensure node passes readiness and pods stabilize.

Cluster stabilization & traffic control:
- If draining many nodes, enable circuit-breaker at ingress/traffic-router level to reduce burst queues.
- Use model fallback routing: route traffic from high-SLO routes to a lower-cap model variant while capacity is rebuilding.
- If autoscaler is configured for Dedicated, ensure scaling policies are not throttled by quotas.

Capacity Add (fast path):
- For immediate capacity: spin up warm spare nodes (if available) or launch pre-baked instance via terraform/ops pipeline: 
   - terraform workspace production; terraform apply -var 'node_pool=emergency-warm' -auto-approve
- For cloud-managed clusters: use nodegroup scale up: aws eks update-nodegroup-config or gcloud container clusters resize commands (follow infra playbook).
- For on-prem: coordinate with infra to boot spare chassis and attach to k8s via bootstrapping script (link to infra runbook in linked_artifacts).

Monitoring & metrics to watch during incident:
- API latency (p50/p95/p99), queue length, token-per-second throughput
- Node-level GPU health metrics: temperature, ecc_errors, pci_errors, driver_restarts
- Pod evictions, restart counts, and scheduling latency
- Cluster level available GPU count (via prometheus query in console)

Post-incident / Incident review notes (what to capture):
- Timeline with exact timestamps for: alert -> cordon -> drain -> HW ticket -> swap -> rejoin -> uncordon
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence (driver bug, thermal event, power distribution, faulty GPU)
- Cost/impact: number of requests dropped, SLO breaches, customer incidents, hours of engineering time
- Action items (owner + due date): firmware updates, upgrade kernel/driver, replace batch of same-model GPUs, add warm spares in region X.

On-call tips & gotchas (notes from recent incidents):
- Don’t assume nvidia-smi is authoritative if driver is partially loaded — check dmesg and journalctl for earlier OOMs.
- Draining can cause transient queuing; notify Product/CS if p95 crosses SLA thresholds.
- If node reboots repeatedly after swap, suspect incompatible firmware or mis-seated power; escalate to Hardware Ops immediately.
- Avoid --force drains on nodes hosting critical stateful services without prior consent.

Command snippets (copyable):
- kubectl cordon node-abc-123
- kubectl drain node-abc-123 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force --grace-period=120
- ssh core@10.70.23.12 'sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 200'
- ssh core@10.70.23.12 'nvidia-smi -q -d MEMORY,UTILIZATION,ERRORS' > /tmp/gpu-dump.txt

Known gaps / TODOs (short list):
- Add automated pre-check that runs on alert to summarize node health & attach to incident channel (SRE-automations).
- Authorize a small set of warm-spare hosts in each AZ for 15-minute cold-start SLA.
- Clarify hardware ops SLA and on-call overlap window (who is first responder after 9pm).
- Create a synthetic test that runs the full drain -> rejoin flow weekly in non-prod.

Revision history:
- 2025-09-12: initial draft (Jordan P.)
- 2025-10-03: clarifications on capacity add and command snippets (Aisha G.)

Notes-to-self: keep this short for pager responders — link to longer Hardware Ops playbook and the SRE incident template. During war-room, one SRE should be the single point of contact to avoid duplicate instructions to HW.

End of doc.
